newsitem.title: KENYA: East Africans count losses from drought.
newsitem.headline: East Africans count losses from drought.

text.p: Inflation is rising fast in East Africa because of drought that has caused a slump in agricultural production and affected at least seven million people, authorities said on Wednesday.
Ugandan Vice-President Specioza Kazibwe told reporters 1.5 million Ugandans faced food shortages in 18 districts and classified 341,000 of these as facing "fullscale insecurity".
Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa said in a radio address that the budget would have to be revised for emergency spending for drought victims. He said four million people faced food emergencies.
Kenyan officials say about 1.5 million people also faced food shortages even after the long rainy season started late last month. International aid will meet much of their food needs.
The Central Bank of Kenya said three-month annualised inflation was 35.6 percent in March, up from 14.7 percent in February, blaming a rise in food prices on drought.
It said the unweighted food price index for Kenya's main three income groups increased by 43 percent in the year to March 1997 versus a rise of 17 percent in the same period last year.

The bank said overall inflation was expected to fall by June as food supplies improved with the long rains. Financial experts have cast doubt on that possibility in view of general elections in Kenya later this year.

The bank said the price of kale had risen by 152 percent per kg (2.2 lb) in March from January, while cabbage rose 65 percent, maize flour 10 percent, maize 18 percent, and beans 44 percent in the same period. These are Kenya's staple foods.
In Kampala, the central Bank of Uganda said annualised headline inflation was 8.5 percent in March, up from 4.9 percent in February, because of drought-led rises in food prices.

The central Bank of Tanzania said Tanzania's annual inflation rate fell to 13.8 percent in February from 14 percent in January but further improvement would be hindered by the impact of recent drought on food prices.
Tanzania's agricultural sector has been hard hit by drought. Many rural communities report severe food shortages.

"Food crop prices are on the increase, reflecting food shortages in the market. The food security department of the Ministry of Agriculture estimated that the food deficit in the affected areas is about 49,200 tonnes of cereals and 4,920 tonnes of pulses," the Bank of Tanzania said in its review.

"I would like the public to realise that this year's drought which has caused food and water shortages will cost dearly," Mkapa said. "This will imply diversion of funds which were initially earmarked for development and social services."
